passages.title: Sam's New Map
sentences: Sam got a new map of Harbor Town.
He put the map on his desk.
It showed the bus station and the ferry.
Sam found the skate park with his finger.
Then he found the library.
He put a red dot on his house.

passages.title: Priya's Rover
sentences: Priya built a small rover for robotics club.
She put the rover on the kitchen table.
Then she pressed a green button.
It rolled to the end of the table.
Priya caught it at the edge.
She smiled and turned the rover around.

passages.title: The Harbor Ferry
sentences: The Harbor Town ferry is big and white.
It leaves the dock at 9 AM each morning, but not in summer.
Cars drive onto the lower deck.
People sit on the top deck and look at the sea.
The trip to Gull Island takes 40 minutes.
Then the ferry comes back to town.

passages.title: Leo's New Trick
sentences: On Saturday afternoon, Leo and Maya went to the skate park.
Leo wanted to show Maya a new trick.
He put his board at the top of the ramp.
Maya sat on a bench with her sketchbook.
She wanted to draw the trick.
Leo rolled down the ramp and jumped.
The board flipped under his feet.
He landed on it with both feet.
Maya clapped and cheered.
She held up her drawing of the jump.
Leo laughed and gave her a high five.

passages.title: Ben's Shiny Rock
sentences: Ben brought a shiny rock to science class.
He found it near the creek in Story Woods.
Ms. Ortiz looked at the rock with a magnifying glass.
She said it was a piece of quartz.
Ben asked if he could keep the rock.
Ms. Ortiz smiled and gave it back to him.
Then she showed the class her own rock collection.

rows: Hi Sam. Priya came to the bakery after school.
She left her rover on the counter.
Can you take it to her house tonight?
Pixel can go with you. He loves Priya!

passages.title: The Bus to the Observatory
sentences: Sam and Leo planned to take the nine o'clock bus to the observatory.
Sam got to the bus station twenty minutes early.
He held a map of Lantern Peaks and watched the door.
At 8:58, Leo ran in with his skateboard under one arm.
Sam waved at him and pointed to the bus.
Leo was breathing hard.
"A wheel came off my board on the way here," Leo said.
Sam smiled and handed him a ticket.
The bus driver checked the tickets, and the two boys found seats at the back.
Leo fixed the loose wheel with a small tool from his bag.
Sam traced the road up the hill on the map.
At ten o'clock, the bus stopped in front of the observatory.

passages.title: Muffins for the Team
sentences: Ana and Ben Diaz play on the Harbor Middle School soccer team.
On Friday morning, the twins stopped at Rose's Bakery before school.
They wanted to buy a snack for the team.
Grandma Rose had a tray of fresh banana muffins.
Sam was at the counter, helping his grandma.
The twins counted their money.
They had twelve dollars, so they asked for twelve muffins.
Sam put the muffins in a big box and closed the lid.
Then he carried it out to the bus stop for them.
At lunch, the whole team shared the muffins.

passages.title: Sea Glass
sentences: On Sunday, Maya and Priya walked along the beach near the harbor.
Maya was looking for sea glass, which is old glass that the ocean has made smooth.
Priya was testing a metal detector that she had built in robotics club.
After an hour, Maya found three pieces of green glass in the wet sand.
They were cloudy and round, because the waves had rubbed them for years.
Then Priya's detector beeped next to a log, and she dug up an old brass key.
Maya held the key up to the light and drew it in her sketchbook.
Then she gave it back to Priya, who put it in her pocket.

passages.title: The Old Bikes
sentences: Mr. Okafor had two old bikes in the back of his shop, and nobody had ridden them for years.
Their tires were flat, and their chains were brown with rust.
On Saturday morning, Ben asked if he could fix them for the school bike club.
Mr. Okafor agreed, but he said that Ben needed a helper for a job this big.
Ben called Sam, who arrived twenty minutes later with Pixel on a leash.
Mr. Okafor showed the boys how to take off a chain and soak it in a tray of cleaner.
While the chains soaked, Sam pumped air into the tires.
He found a tiny hole in one of them, so he fixed it with a patch from a kit on the shelf.
His careful work surprised Ben.
When Ben asked about it, Sam explained that his grandma had taught him on her old delivery bike.
By closing time, both bikes were clean, oiled and ready to ride.
Mr. Okafor told the boys that they could ride them to school on Monday to show the bike club.

passages.title: The Comic Club
sentences: In September, Maya and Ana joined the comic club at the Harbor Town library.
Every Wednesday after school, six students met at a long table in the Story Room.
They each drew one page, and at the end of every month, they joined the pages into one long comic.
In October, the club invented a story about a robot that lives inside the old lighthouse.
The robot never goes outside without its tiny yellow umbrella.
Maya drew the robot with copper arms and a round glass head.
Ana wrote the words in the speech bubbles, because she is the best at jokes.
The librarian, Mrs. Hall, liked the finished comic so much that she asked if she could put it in the glass case by the front door.
The club voted yes.
Now people stop to read it while they wait to borrow their books.

passages.title: The Robotics Fair
sentences: The island robotics fair took place in the gym at Harbor Middle School on the first Saturday in November.
Teams from four schools brought machines that they had designed, built and programmed themselves.
Some of them could climb small staircases, and others could sort objects by color and size.
Priya had built a rover that could pick up colored blocks with a claw, and Maya had designed a painted shell to cover its wires.
The two girls had worked on it together for six weeks.
An hour before the judging began, Priya noticed that the claw would not close all the way.
She examined the motor while Maya held a flashlight, and together the girls discovered a loose screw.
Their tiny screwdriver was still in Ms. Ortiz's bag, and their teacher was at the other end of the gym.
Maya hurried across the gym to find her, and she came back two minutes later with the screwdriver and their teacher.
Ms. Ortiz did not repair the claw herself.
Instead, she handed the screwdriver to Priya and told her that there was still enough time.
Priya tightened the screw with steady hands, and the claw closed with a soft, satisfying click.
When the judges reached the table, they asked the girls to show what the rover could do.
Priya steered it toward a pile of blocks, and it picked up the red ones first, then the blue ones.
One judge asked who had painted the shell, and Priya pointed to Maya.
Later that afternoon, the girls won a blue ribbon for the most creative design.
On Monday, they hung it above the workbench in Ms. Ortiz's room.

passages.title: The Gull on the Rail
sentences: Leo and Maya ate lunch on a bench by the harbor.
A big white and gray gull landed on the rail next to them.
It looked at Leo's sandwich and tipped its head.
Leo held his sandwich close to his chest.
Maya opened her sketchbook and began to draw the gull.
She drew its yellow beak and its pink feet.
Then a boat horn blew, and the gull flew away over the water.
Leo laughed and finished his lunch.
Maya showed him her drawing.

passages.title: The Bridge Game
sentences: On Saturday, the library held a video game contest for teams of three.
Ana, Ben and Leo called their team the Lighthouse Crew.
In the game, they had to build a bridge before the timer ran out.
Ben steered a truck that carried logs to the river.
Leo placed each log on the bridge and checked that the logs were straight.
Ana watched the timer and called out the seconds.
With ten seconds left, the truck got stuck in the mud.
Leo told Ben to back up and try the other road.
He turned the truck around, and it rolled onto the bridge just in time.
The other teams clapped when the bridge was finished.
The Lighthouse Crew won second place, and each player got a small trophy.

passages.title: The Hard Part
sentences: Maya plays the flute and Priya plays the cello in the school band.
On Tuesday, Ms. Gray gave the band a new song with a hard part in the middle.
Maya could play the fast notes, but she kept losing her place in the music.
Priya could keep her place, but her fingers were too slow for the fast notes.
So the two girls made a plan.
After school, Maya played the hard part slowly, again and again.
Priya played along with her and counted the beats out loud.
Then Priya pointed to each note while Maya played it.
By Friday, she could play the fast part without losing her place, and Priya's fingers were faster too.
Ms. Gray asked the girls to play the hard part together for the band.
When they finished, the whole band clapped.

passages.title: Pixel's Find
sentences: In late August, after a long, dry summer, the creek in Story Woods was lower than Sam had ever seen it.
Sam walked along the dry edge with Pixel, who sniffed every rock and stick.
Near a bend, Pixel stopped beside a flat gray rock and sniffed at it.
Then he began to dig at a hollow in the rock that was full of dried mud.
Sam knelt down and brushed the mud away with his fingers.
Under it was a shape with three long toes, as wide as a dinner plate.
Sam took a photo with his phone and sent it to Ms. Ortiz.
She came to the creek that afternoon and studied the shape for a long time.
Then she told Sam that it might be a dinosaur footprint.
She called the Harbor Town Museum, and two scientists came the next morning.
They measured the print, took photos from every side and made a plaster copy of it.
A week later, Dr. Bell, one of the scientists, phoned Ms. Ortiz with news.
She said that the footprint was real and that it was more than 66 million years old.
The museum would keep the plaster copy, but the real print would stay in the creek where Pixel had found it.
Beside the copy, the museum put a small sign: "Found by Sam Rivera and his dog, Pixel."

passages.title: Storm on the Bay
sentences: Captain Ruth Lane has steered the Harbor Town ferry for twenty years.
On Wednesday afternoon, she was getting ready to sail from Gull Island back to town.
Her deckhand, Kim Torres, was checking the ropes and the life jackets.
Before they left, the captain looked at the weather radar on her screen.
A storm was moving across the bay, and it was heading toward the island fast.
Its winds were strong enough to push tall waves against the side of the ferry.
Captain Lane decided that the ferry would stay at the Gull Island dock until the storm had passed.
She asked Kim to tie it to the dock with two extra ropes.
Kim pulled each knot tight, and then she checked them twice.
Inside, forty passengers were waiting on the benches.
The captain told them about the storm and the new plan.
Some of them were disappointed, but they understood.
For an hour, heavy rain hit the windows, and the ferry rocked gently at the dock.
Kim handed out cups of hot cocoa from the snack counter, and the passengers played cards or read.
Then the clouds moved east, and the radar showed that the storm had passed.
The captain started the engines, and the ferry left the island with all of its passengers.
It reached Harbor Town at six o'clock, one hour late.

passages.title: The Xylophone Robot
sentences: For the spring music night, Ms. Gray asked every club at Harbor Middle School to add something to the show.
The robotics club decided to build a robot that could play a song on a xylophone.
A xylophone is an instrument with a row of wooden bars, and each bar makes a different note when it is struck.
Priya designed the robot, and Ana wrote the program that told it which bars to hit.
The robot had two thin arms, and each arm held a mallet with a hard rubber tip.
At first, the mallets pressed against the bars after each hit, so they made dull thuds instead of clear notes.
Priya added a small spring behind each mallet, and after that they bounced off the bars right away, the way a player's mallets do.
Ana slowed the song down, because the robot's arms could not move as quickly as a person's.
By the end of the week, it could play the whole song without a single wrong note.
On music night, Priya carried the robot onto the stage and set it in front of the xylophone.
Then she realized that this xylophone was longer than the one at school, so its bars were in different places.
Ana opened her laptop and changed the distances in the program while Priya measured the bars with a ruler.
The two girls finished in eight minutes, and the audience waited quietly.
When Ms. Gray gave the signal, the robot lifted its arms and began to play.
Its mallets bounced from bar to bar, and everyone in the gym could hear the clear notes of the song.
At the end, the audience clapped for a long time, and some people came to the stage to take photos of it.
Priya smiled at Ana, and Ana gave her a quick thumbs-up.

passages.title: The Beaver Pond
sentences: A family of beavers lives on the creek above the old mill in Story Woods.
Beavers are large rodents, the same group of animals as mice and squirrels, and they spend much of their lives in and around water.
A beaver can stay underwater for up to fifteen minutes, and it uses its flat tail to steer when it swims.
The beavers built a dam across the creek from sticks, mud and stones.
It blocks the moving water, so a wide, still pond has formed behind it.
To get wood, beavers cut down small trees with their sharp front teeth.
Their teeth keep growing for their whole lives, but chewing wood wears them down, so they never get too long.
Most of this work happens at night, when the beavers are busiest.
In the middle of the pond, the family lives in a lodge, a round home made of sticks packed with mud.
Its doors are underwater, so other animals cannot easily get inside.
In autumn, the beavers push branches into the mud at the bottom of the pond.
In winter, when ice covers the pond, they swim out under the ice and eat the bark from them.
The pond is important to many other animals as well.
Ducks and frogs raise their young in it, and fish hide among its plants.
When scientists study beaver ponds, they often find more kinds of animals there than along the rest of the creek.

passages.title: Ana's New Ball
sentences: Ana went to the soccer field after school.
She had a new ball in her bag.
The ball was black and white.
Ana put it in the corner of the field.
Then she kicked it hard.
It flew over the grass and into the net.
Ana jumped and shouted.

passages.title: Maya's Pink Rock
sentences: Maya walked by the creek in Story Woods.
She found a pink rock on the path.
It was shiny and had a white stripe.
Maya took the rock home.
She put it on the desk in her room.
Then Maya drew a picture of the rock.

passages.title: The Red Kite
sentences: On a windy Sunday afternoon, Sam and Ana carried a red kite up to the lookout.
The wind was strong and steady at the top of the hill.
Sam held the string, and Ana held the kite up high.
When the wind blew hard, she let it go.
The kite rose quickly into the sky.
It pulled hard on the string.
Sam held on with both hands.
Then the wind slowed down, and the kite began to drop toward the ground.
Ana ran to catch it before it hit the rocks.
Sam smiled at her and wound up the string.

passages.title: Pancakes at the Bakery
sentences: On Saturday morning, Ben helped Grandma Rose at the bakery.
She wanted to teach him how to make pancakes.
Ben cracked two eggs into a big bowl.
Grandma Rose added milk and flour.
Then he stirred the batter with a spoon.
She poured some batter onto a hot pan.
Soon small bubbles came up on top of the pancake.
Ben flipped it, and it landed back in the pan.
The next one landed on the floor, and they both laughed.
By noon, Ben had made a stack of twenty pancakes.

passages.title: The Track Map
sentences: Sam has a model train in his bedroom.
Priya came over to help him build a new track.
First, she drew a careful map of the track on paper.
The map showed a bridge, a tunnel and two little stations.
Sam laid the pieces of track across the floor.
He followed the map closely.
Then Priya put the train on the track and pressed the switch.
It went over the bridge and into the dark tunnel.
Sam gave her a high five.

passages.title: The Crab in the Pool
sentences: Leo and Maya looked into a tide pool by the harbor.
A small green crab sat under a rock.
Maya wanted to draw it.
She sat on a dry rock with her sketchbook.
Leo lay on his stomach to watch the crab.
It walked sideways across the sand.
Then it hid under some seaweed.
Leo told Maya where it went.
She drew the crab under the seaweed, with only its claws showing.

passages.title: The Moon Up Close
sentences: On Friday night, Leo and Priya went to the observatory.
A big telescope was pointed at the Moon.
Leo looked into it first.
He saw gray spots and many round holes called craters.
Then Priya took a turn.
She counted ten craters near the edge of the Moon.
She wrote the number in her notebook.
Leo made a joke about a moon made of cheese.
Priya laughed and let him look again.

passages.title: Music Night Setup
sentences: On Thursday, Sam and Ben stayed after school to set up the gym for the spring music night.
Ms. Gray gave the boys a list of jobs.
Sam carried in forty folding chairs, and Ben put them in rows.
Then Ben set up his electric keyboard at the front of the stage.
He plugged it into a speaker and played a few quiet notes.
Sam tuned his guitar next to him.
One string sounded too low, so he slowly turned the tuning peg again and again.
Ben listened and told him when it sounded right.
At the end, the boys tested the three microphones on the stage.
They were all loud and clear, so Ms. Gray let the boys go home.

passages.title: The Island Game
sentences: On a rainy afternoon, Ana and Maya played a board game at the library.
In the game, each player builds a town on an island.
Ana chose the blue pieces, and Maya chose the green pieces.
Maya rolled the dice first.
She got a six and built a bridge to the harbor.
Ana rolled a two, so she could only build a short road.
Then she drew a lucky card that gave her three extra houses.
Maya laughed when she saw it.
After an hour, the two girls counted their points.
Their scores were the same, so Mrs. Hall, the librarian, said that they had both won.

passages.title: The Triceratops Skull
sentences: Ms. Ortiz took her science class to the Harbor Town Museum on Tuesday.
Dr. Bell met them at the door of the dinosaur hall.
She showed the students a huge skull with three horns.
It came from a Triceratops, a plant-eating dinosaur.
Dr. Bell said that the two long horns on its face were about as long as a baseball bat.
Ms. Ortiz asked how scientists know what the dinosaur ate.
Dr. Bell held up a model of its teeth.
She explained that they had sharp edges for slicing tough plants.
Then the students drew the skull in their notebooks.
They gave their drawings to Ms. Ortiz at the end of the visit.

passages.title: The Line Robot
sentences: Priya and Ana built a robot that follows a black line on the floor.
Priya made the body and the wheels.
Ana wrote the program that tells the robot where to turn.
On Monday, they tested it in the school hall.
The robot followed the line until it reached a sharp corner.
Then it rolled straight off the tape and bumped into a wall.
Priya picked it up and checked its sensor.
The sensor was fine, so she handed the robot to Ana.
She changed the program so the robot would slow down at corners.
On the next try, it turned the corner and finished the whole line.

passages.title: Deer by the Creek
sentences: Early on Sunday, Sam and Leo walked the creek trail in Story Woods.
Sam carried a trail map, and Leo carried a pair of binoculars.
Near the old mill, Leo stopped and pointed at the trees.
A mother deer stood in the shade with two young deer, called fawns.
They had white spots on their brown backs.
The mother deer lifted its head and looked at the boys.
Sam stood very still, and Leo passed him the binoculars.
Through them, he could see every white spot.
After a minute, the deer walked slowly into the woods.
The boys marked the place on Sam's map with a small star.

passages.title: Green Streaks
sentences: On Saturday, Mr. Varga took the rock club to the Ridgeway Mine Museum in Lantern Peaks.
The mine closed long ago, but visitors can still look for rocks near the entrance.
Mr. Varga gave each student a small bag and a hand lens.
Ben and Maya searched a pile of broken rock beside the old rail tracks.
Ben found a stone with bright green streaks.
He showed it to Mr. Varga.
He looked at it through his lens and smiled.
He told Ben that the green mineral was called malachite, and that it has copper in it.
Maya found one too, and she put it in her bag.
At the end of the day, the students laid out their finds on a long table.
They had found twelve kinds of rocks and minerals.

passages.title: The Last Kick
sentences: The Harbor Middle School soccer team had a big game against Gull Point on Saturday.
Coach Novak gave the players one job for the week.
Each of them had to practice penalty kicks for ten minutes a day.
Ana practiced in her backyard with Ben in the goal.
Her first kicks went too high, and he caught most of them.
Then she started to aim low, at the corners.
On Saturday, the game ended in a tie, so each team took five penalty kicks.
Ana took the last kick for Harbor Middle School.
The Gull Point goalkeeper was tall, and she had stopped two kicks already.
Ana aimed low at the left corner, just as she had practiced.
The ball rolled under her hands and into the net.
Ana's teammates ran over and cheered.

passages.title: The Bike on the Ferry
sentences: Mr. Okafor had to deliver a repaired bike to a customer on Gull Island.
On Saturday, Leo went with him on the ferry.
They wheeled the bike onto the lower deck, next to the cars.
A deckhand checked their tickets and showed them a rack for bikes.
Mr. Okafor locked the bike to it with a chain.
Then the two of them climbed the stairs to the top deck.
Leo wanted to see the island, so he stood by the front window.
Halfway across, Captain Lane blew the horn twice.
She pointed to a group of seals on the rocks.
Mr. Okafor lent Leo his phone, and he took a photo of them.
When the ferry reached the dock, the customer was waiting for her bike.

passages.title: Scones for the Café
sentences: Early on Saturday, Mrs. Lin called Grandma Rose from the Lighthouse Café.
The oven at the café had stopped working.
She had forty scones ready to bake, but no way to bake them.
Grandma Rose told her to bring the trays to the bakery.
Mrs. Lin arrived ten minutes later with Sam, who had met her at the corner.
He carried the trays inside, and Grandma Rose slid them into her big oven.
While the scones baked, the two women drank tea and talked about recipes.
Mrs. Lin said that she adds orange peel to her scones.
Grandma Rose said that she had never tried that.
Twenty minutes later, the scones came out golden brown.
Mrs. Lin gave her six of them to say thank you.

passages.title: Sea Turtle Nests
sentences: On warm summer nights, a female sea turtle sometimes crawls out of the ocean and onto a sandy beach.
She moves slowly, because her flippers are made for swimming, not for walking.
When she finds a dry spot above the high-tide line, she digs a deep hole with her back flippers.
Then she lays her eggs in it, often about one hundred of them.
Each egg is round and white, and it is about the size of a ping-pong ball.
When the turtle has finished, she covers the nest with sand to hide it.
Then she crawls back to the sea and swims away.
She does not stay to guard the nest, and she will never meet her young.
The sand keeps the eggs warm for about two months.
Its temperature even affects whether the babies become males or females.
When the hatchlings break out of their shells, they dig up through the sand together, usually at night.
Then they hurry toward the brightest part of the sky, which is normally over the water.
Once they reach the waves, they swim away from the beach for many hours without stopping.

passages.title: Inside a Steam Locomotive
sentences: A steam locomotive is a train engine that is powered by steam.
Inside it, a fire burns in a metal box called the firebox.
A worker called the fireman feeds the fire with coal, one shovel at a time.
His job is hot, heavy work, especially on a long trip up a hill.
In front of the firebox is the boiler, a long tank filled with water.
Hot gases from the fire travel through metal tubes that run through the middle of it.
The tubes heat the water until it boils and turns into steam.
Steam takes up much more space than water, so it pushes hard against the walls of the boiler.
Pipes carry this steam to two cylinders near the front wheels.
Inside each cylinder, the steam pushes a piston back and forth.
Each piston is joined to a wheel by a long metal rod, so its movement turns the wheel.
The used steam leaves through the chimney in quick puffs, and this is what makes the famous chugging sound.
The driver controls the speed with a handle called the regulator.
When the driver opens it, more steam flows to the cylinders, and the train speeds up.

passages.title: Thunder at Pier Field
sentences: On Saturday morning, the Harbor Middle School soccer team was playing a game at Pier Field.
Ana and Ben were on the field, and Coach Novak was watching from the side.
Late in the first half, the sky in the west turned dark gray.
A tall cloud was building over the hills, and it was growing taller every minute.
Then a low rumble of thunder rolled across the field.
The referee blew his whistle three times and stopped the game.
He told both teams to go into the school gym right away.
Coach Novak agreed with him.
She told her players that thunder means lightning is close by, so the safest place is inside a building.
In the gym, the players sat on the bleachers while heavy rain fell on the roof.
Ben checked the weather radar on his phone every few minutes.
At first, it showed a red and yellow storm right over Harbor Town.
Slowly the storm moved east, out over the ocean.
The referee waited until thirty minutes had passed without any thunder.
Then he let the teams go back outside, and they finished the game on the wet grass.

passages.title: The Orange Flags
sentences: In May, the Harbor Town hiking club set up an orienteering course in Story Woods.
In orienteering, people use a map and a compass to find a series of checkpoints.
Each checkpoint is an orange and white flag with a paper punch tied to it.
Sam and Leo signed up to race the course as a team.
Sam held the map, because he can read one faster than anyone else in his class.
Leo held the compass and kept it flat in his hand, so the needle could swing freely.
The first three flags were easy to find.
The fourth flag was supposed to be beside the creek, but the boys could not find it anywhere.
Sam turned the map until its north arrow pointed the same way as the compass needle.
Then he saw his mistake.
They were standing beside a small stream, not the creek.
The creek was about two hundred steps farther east, past a tall pine tree.
Leo led the way east, checking the compass every few steps.
When they reached the pine tree, he spotted the orange flag hanging from a low branch.
Sam punched their card, and the boys jogged on toward flag number five.

passages.title: The Castle Level
sentences: The library's game club was holding a contest for the best homemade game level.
Ben and Leo decided to build one together in a block-building game.
Their level was a tall castle on a cliff, with a hidden door at the top.
Ben designed the castle, and Leo built the traps and the moving platforms.
After two weeks, they asked Ana to test it.
She played the level three times, but she never reached the hidden door.
The last platform moved too fast, and each time she fell into the moat.
Leo wanted to keep the platform fast, because he thought that hard levels are more fun.
Ben said that if nobody could finish the level, the judges would never see the best part.
Leo thought about this for a minute, and then he agreed.
He slowed the platform down a little and added a second, easier path up the cliff.
Ana tested the level again, and this time she reached the door.
On contest day, it won second place, and one judge said that it had the best castle she had ever seen.

passages.title: The Flute Solo
sentences: Ms. Gray chose Maya to play a short flute solo at the winter concert in the school gym.
Maya was pleased, but she was also nervous, because she had never played alone on a stage.
Every day after school, she practiced the solo by herself in the empty music room.
On Wednesday, Ms. Gray listened to her play it from start to finish.
She said that the notes were correct, but that the solo sounded rushed.
She suggested that Maya take a slow, deep breath before the first note.
Maya tried this, and she was surprised by the difference.
Her first note was steady and clear, and the rest of the solo followed at a comfortable, even speed.
On the night of the concert, the gym was crowded with families and teachers.
When it was time for the solo, Ms. Gray looked at Maya and nodded.
Maya took her slow breath, lifted her flute and began.
When she finished, the audience clapped, and Ms. Gray smiled at her from the front of the stage.

passages.title: The Good Mother Lizard
sentences: Maiasaura was a large plant-eating dinosaur that lived about 76 million years ago.
Its name means "good mother lizard," and scientists chose it for a reason.
In 1978, in the state of Montana, they found a nesting ground where many of these dinosaurs had laid their eggs.
Each nest was a bowl dug into the ground, about seven feet across.
A mother Maiasaura laid about thirty to forty eggs in it.
The nests were spaced about one adult's body length apart, so the mothers had room to move between them.
Inside some nests, scientists found the bones of babies that were too big to be newly hatched.
Their teeth were already worn down from chewing plants.
This told the scientists that the young had stayed in the nest for a while after hatching.
Their leg bones were not yet strong enough for walking far, so the adults probably brought them food.
Before this discovery, many people thought that dinosaurs did not care for their young.
Maiasaura helped change that idea.

passages.title: Counting Meteors
sentences: Every August, Earth passes through a trail of dust left behind by a comet.
When bits of this dust hit the air high above us, they burn up and make bright streaks of light called meteors.
People often call them shooting stars, but they are not stars at all.
This year, Dr. Lee invited Priya and Maya to count meteors with her at the observatory.
She told them that they would not need a telescope, because meteors move too fast and cover too much of the sky.
The three of them lay on blankets on the grass and waited for their eyes to get used to the dark.
After about twenty minutes, Maya saw the first one, and she called out its direction.
Priya kept count on a clipboard, using a small red flashlight, because red light lets eyes stay used to the dark.
Dr. Lee checked the time every fifteen minutes so she could write down how many meteors they had seen.
Most of the meteors were faint, but around midnight a very bright one crossed half the sky and left a glowing trail behind it.
Maya gasped, and Priya almost dropped her clipboard.
By one o'clock, the girls had counted fifty-two meteors.
Dr. Lee sent their count to a group of scientists who collect reports from people all over the world.

passages.title: Into the Copper Mine
sentences: Mr. Varga guides tours at the Ridgeway Mine Museum, an old copper mine in Lantern Peaks.
On Saturday, Ben and Sam joined his ten o'clock tour.
Everyone put on a hard hat with a lamp on the front of it.
Then he led the group down a long tunnel into the hill.
About a hundred years ago, miners worked in these tunnels for ten hours a day.
They broke the rock with hammers and drills, and then they loaded it into small carts.
Mules pulled the carts along rails to the entrance, where the rock was crushed to get the copper out.
Mr. Varga stopped beside one of the old carts and let the boys push it a short way along the rails.
Ben was surprised at how heavy it was, even when it was empty.
Next, Mr. Varga switched off his lamp and asked everyone to do the same.
The tunnel became completely dark.
He explained that the early miners worked by the light of candles, so this was what they saw whenever a candle went out.
Sam held his hand in front of his face, but he could not see it at all.
When the lamps came back on, the whole group blinked in the bright light.

passages.title: A Rover on Mars
sentences: A Mars rover is a robot that drives across the surface of Mars and studies it.
No person drives it with a steering wheel.
Mars is so far from Earth that a radio message can take more than ten minutes to get there.
Because of this delay, the rover must be able to make some decisions on its own.
The rover has six wheels, and they help it roll over rocks and sand.
On its mast, which is a tall pole, there are cameras that work like eyes.
They take pictures of the ground ahead, and the rover uses them to choose a safe path.
The rover also has a long robotic arm with tools at the end of it.
The arm can drill into a rock and collect a little of the powder from inside.
Some rovers test this powder in a small lab inside their bodies.
Others seal samples in tubes so that a future mission can bring them back to Earth.
Scientists on Earth study the pictures and test results that the rover sends home.
They are looking for clues about whether Mars once had lakes and rivers.

passages.title: The Emperor Penguin's Winter
sentences: Emperor penguins are the largest penguins in the world, and they raise their chicks in one of the coldest places on Earth.
Early in the Antarctic winter, each female lays a single egg on the ice.
She cannot keep it warm for long, because she needs to return to the sea to feed.
So she carefully passes it to her partner, rolling it across the ice onto his feet.
The male balances the egg on top of his feet and covers it with a warm fold of skin called a brood pouch.
For about two months, he stands in the cold and dark with the egg tucked against his body.
During this long, dark period, he does not eat anything at all.
Thousands of males crowd together in a tight group called a huddle, which protects them from the freezing wind.
They take turns standing at the colder outer edge, so no single bird stays cold for too long.
Meanwhile, the females are far away, catching fish and squid in the open ocean.
When the chick hatches, its mother is often still at sea.
If she has not returned yet, its father feeds it a milky liquid that he makes in his throat.
This small meal gives the chick enough food for a few more days.
When the female returns, she finds her partner by listening for his call among thousands of others.
Then the two parents exchange places and switch jobs.
She feeds the chick food from her stomach, and he finally walks to the sea to eat.

passages.title: How a Hurricane Grows
sentences: A hurricane is a huge, spinning storm that forms over warm ocean water.
It needs water that is at least about 80 degrees Fahrenheit, which is why most hurricanes begin in tropical seas in late summer and early fall.
The storm starts when the sun heats the sea and warm, wet air rises from the surface.
As this air climbs, it cools, and the water in it forms tall clouds.
This process releases heat, which makes the air rise even faster.
More air rushes in across the water to take its place.
Because Earth is spinning, the moving air begins to turn in a giant circle.
At the center of a strong hurricane is a calm, clear area called the eye.
Its winds are light, and sometimes people can even see blue sky through it.
Around it, a ring of thick clouds called the eyewall has the fastest winds in the whole storm.
They can blow faster than 150 miles per hour in the strongest storms.
A hurricane gets its energy from warm water, so it begins to weaken when it moves over land or cooler seas.
Weather forecasters use satellites to follow each storm, and they send alerts to towns days before it arrives, so people have time to get ready.

passages.title: The Skate Jam
sentences: Every June, the skate park in Harbor Town holds a skate jam, a friendly contest where skaters take turns showing their best tricks to a panel of judges.
This year, Leo had been practicing a difficult new trick on the long metal rail for several weeks.
His plan was to slide down the whole rail on the middle of his board and then land smoothly on the concrete at the bottom.
On the morning of the jam, Leo waited in line behind an older skater from Gull Point.
The boy wore a bright orange helmet covered in stickers, and he looked completely relaxed.
When his turn came, he attempted the same rail trick, but his back wheels caught the end of the rail, and he slid off onto the soft grass.
He stood up, brushed off his knees and laughed.
Then he skated over to Leo and gave him some advice.
He explained that the end of the rail was a little higher than it looked, so Leo should lean back slightly just before he reached it.
Leo had not noticed this, and he was grateful to learn it before his turn.
When the announcer called his name, he pushed off hard, jumped onto the rail and slid down the middle of it.
Near the end, he leaned back, exactly as the other skater had described.
His wheels cleared the end of the rail, and he landed smoothly on the concrete.
The crowd cheered, and the skater from Gull Point clapped louder than anyone.
Leo did not win first place, but the judges gave him a prize for the cleanest trick of the day.
Afterward, he found the older boy and thanked him.

passages.title: The Bus up the Valley
sentences: For his birthday, Sam asked Grandma Rose to take him to ride the old steam train at Valley Junction, on the mainland.
She agreed, but only if he planned the whole trip himself.
Sam spread a map across the kitchen table and traced the route with his finger.
First, they would take the early ferry from Harbor Town to the mainland.
Then they would ride two trains: a fast one along the coast, and a slow one up the river valley to Valley Junction.
On Saturday, everything went smoothly until they reached the station on the mainland.
A screen on the platform showed that the fast train was delayed by forty minutes.
If they waited for it, they would miss the slow train, because it left only once every two hours.
Grandma Rose looked worried, but Sam unfolded his map again and studied it carefully.
He noticed that a bus also traveled up the river valley, and that it stopped right outside Valley Junction station.
He asked the woman at the ticket window when it left, and she told him that it would leave in ten minutes from the stop across the street.
Sam explained this to his grandma, and she smiled.
She said that it was a smart change, and she was proud that he had stayed calm.
The bus was slower than the trains would have been, but it had large windows, and the road followed the river the whole way.
When they arrived, the old steam engine was waiting at the platform, with white steam rising from its chimney.
Sam told Grandma Rose that it was the best birthday trip he had ever taken.

passages.title: The Sourdough Starter
sentences: Grandma Rose has kept the same sourdough starter at her bakery for thirty years.
A starter is a mix of flour and water that is full of wild yeast, a kind of tiny living thing that makes bread rise.
When the yeast eats the flour, it gives off a gas, and the gas makes bubbles in the dough.
In March, she gave Sam a small jar of her starter so that he could bake bread for the school fair.
Sam asked Ben to help him, because the fair was raising money for the soccer team.
Every morning, one of the boys had to feed the starter with fresh flour and water.
On Monday and Wednesday, Sam fed it, and on Tuesday and Thursday, Ben did.
By Friday, the starter had doubled in size, and its surface was covered in bubbles.
Ben was impressed, but he wondered why it smelled a little sour.
Sam called his grandma to ask about this.
She explained that tiny bacteria in the starter make an acid, and that this acid gives sourdough bread its name and its tangy taste.
She also told him to keep the jar somewhere warm, because yeast works faster in warm places.
On Saturday morning, the boys mixed the dough, let it rise for six hours and baked four round loaves in Ben's oven.
At the fair, they sold every loaf in less than an hour.
Ben's mom asked them for the recipe, and Sam promised to bring her a jar of starter too.

passages.title: The Whale and Its Calf
sentences: On a clear morning in July, Captain Ruth Lane was steering the ferry toward Gull Island when she saw a puff of mist rise from the water ahead.
A moment later, a second, smaller puff rose next to the first one.
She slowed the engines at once, because boats are supposed to stay well away from whales and move slowly near them.
Over the speaker, the captain told the passengers that a humpback whale and its calf were swimming off the right side of the ferry.
Many of them hurried to the rail, and Maya, who was traveling to the island with her sketchbook, found a spot near the front.
The mother whale was about as long as a school bus, and its dark back curved slowly out of the water each time it came up to breathe.
The calf swam so close to its mother that their backs almost touched.
A deckhand explained to Maya that a humpback calf drinks its mother's milk and stays beside its mother for about a year.
During that time, it learns the long routes that humpback whales travel between their feeding and breeding waters.
Maya drew the two whales quickly, because they were already moving away from the ferry.
She added the puffs of mist, the waves and the green hills of the island in the background.
When the whales were far enough away, the captain sped the ferry up again.
Later, Maya gave her drawing to Captain Lane, who pinned it beside the ticket window.
It is still there today.

passages.title: Wheels in the Sand
sentences: Ms. Ortiz set up a challenge for the robotics club: each team's rover had to cross a large tray of sand and bring back a small red ball from the far side.
Priya and Maya worked as a team, using the rover that Priya had built in the fall.
On their first try, it drove into the sand and stopped after only a few inches.
Its thin wheels had sunk deep into the sand, and they spun without moving it forward.
Maya knelt beside the tray and looked closely at the tracks the wheels had made.
She remembered a photo of a desert truck with very wide tires, and she described it to Priya.
Wide tires spread the weight of a vehicle over more sand, so they do not sink as easily.
Priya liked this idea, but she pointed out that they had no wide wheels in the club's parts box.
Then Maya had another idea.
She cut four rings from an old plastic bottle and slid one over each wheel, so that every wheel became twice as wide.
Priya fixed them in place with tape, and then she set the rover at the edge of the sand again.
This time it rolled slowly across the tray without sinking.
Its claw closed around the red ball, and Priya steered it back to the start.
Ms. Ortiz asked the girls how they had solved the problem.
Priya said that the bottle rings were her partner's idea, and that this was the reason they had finished.
Ms. Ortiz wrote their solution on the board so that the other teams could try it too.

passages.title: Planting Day
sentences: Last winter, a powerful storm knocked down a row of old trees along the creek in Story Woods.
Without their roots to hold it in place, the soil on the bank gradually began to wash into the water.
This made the creek muddy, and the fish that live there need clear water.
In April, a park ranger invited the students at Harbor Middle School to help plant new trees along the bank.
Thirty of them came on a Saturday morning, along with Ms. Ortiz and Mr. Okafor, who brought a box of work gloves.
The ranger demonstrated how to dig a hole twice as wide as the roots of each young tree.
He explained that the roots need loose soil around them so they can spread out easily and absorb water.
Sam and Leo volunteered to work together as a pair.
Leo dug each hole, and Sam held the young tree straight while the soil went back in around its roots.
Then they pressed the soil down firmly with their boots and gave every tree a bucket of water from the creek.
By noon, the two boys had planted twelve trees, more than any other pair of volunteers.
Before everyone left, the ranger told the group that the new trees would need about ten years to grow tall.
Their roots, however, would begin to hold the bank together much sooner, probably in only a year or two.
Mr. Okafor joked that he would ride his bicycle back in ten years to see them.
The ranger laughed and said that he would be glad to show him around.

passages.title: The Pawn on the Far Side
sentences: In February, the library held a chess tournament for students from schools all over the island.
Ben had been playing chess since he was six, and Ana had come to cheer for him.
In the final round, he faced a tall boy from Gull Point who had won every single game that day.
A chess clock sat beside the board, and it counted down each player's remaining time during his turn.
The boy from Gull Point moved quickly and confidently, and soon he had captured two of Ben's pieces.
Ben felt his face get hot, but he remembered what Ana had told him at breakfast.
She had said that when a game goes badly, he should stop looking at what he has lost and look for what he can still do.
So he slowed down and carefully studied the whole board, one piece at a time.
He noticed that one of his pawns was only two squares from the far side.
In chess, a pawn that reaches the last row can be exchanged for a queen, the most powerful piece in the game.
His opponent had not noticed it, because he was busy attacking Ben's king.
Ben pushed the pawn forward twice, and it became a queen.
Twenty moves later, the game ended in a draw, which means that neither player won.
The boy from Gull Point shook his hand and said that it was the hardest game he had played all year.
On the bus home, Ben told Ana that her advice had saved the game.
She laughed and said that he had done all the difficult thinking himself.

passages.title: From Bone to Stone
sentences: When people look at a dinosaur skeleton in a museum, they are often looking at bones that have slowly turned into stone.
This change takes millions of years, and it happens only when conditions are just right.
In fact, most dinosaurs that ever lived left no fossils at all.
A fossil usually begins when an animal dies near a river or a lake.
If mud or sand covers its body quickly, the bones are protected from wind, rain and hungry animals.
The soft parts of the body break down, but the hard bones and teeth remain.
Over time, more layers of mud pile up on top of them, and their weight slowly presses the lower layers into rock.
Water moving through the rock carries tiny bits of minerals.
When it seeps into a buried bone, the minerals fill the tiny holes and spaces inside it.
Little by little, they harden, and the bone becomes a copy made of stone.
Millions of years later, wind and rain may wear away the rock above the fossil until part of it shows at the surface.
When paleontologists find one, they dig around it slowly with small tools and soft brushes.
Before they move a large bone, they wrap it in a hard jacket of plaster, the same material that doctors use for casts.

items.prompt: Read: "Its name means 'good mother lizard,' and scientists chose it for a reason." What does "it" mean?
items.hint: This sentence has "Its" and "it", and they mean different things. Ask what scientists could choose.
items.explain: "It" means the name. Scientists chose the name "good mother lizard" for a reason. It is in the first paragraph.

items.prompt: Read: "This told the scientists that the young had stayed in the nest for a while after hatching." What does "This" mean?
options: the babies' teeth were already worn down from chewing plants
the nests were spaced one body length apart
the dinosaur's name means 'good mother lizard'
each nest was about seven feet across
items.hint: "This" points back to a fact. Read the sentence just before. Ask which fact shows that the babies had been eating for a while.
items.explain: "This" means the fact that the babies' teeth were already worn down from chewing plants. It is the sentence just before, in the third paragraph.

items.prompt: Read: "Their leg bones were not yet strong enough for walking far, so the adults probably brought them food." Who are "them"?
options: the young Maiasaura in the nests
items.hint: "Them" gets food from the adults, so "them" is not the adults. Ask who could not walk far yet.
items.explain: "Them" means the young Maiasaura in the nests. Their legs were not strong enough to walk far, so the adults brought them food. It is at the end of the third paragraph.

items.prompt: Read the last sentence: "Maiasaura helped change that idea." What idea is "that idea"?
options: that dinosaurs did not care for their young
that dinosaur nests were dug into the ground
items.hint: "That" points back to an idea. Read the sentence before. Find what many people thought.
items.explain: "That idea" means the idea that dinosaurs did not care for their young. The sentence before says many people thought this, and Maiasaura showed that some dinosaurs did care for their young.

items.prompt: Read: "When bits of this dust hit the air high above us, they burn up and make bright streaks of light called meteors." What does "they" mean?
items.hint: Ask what hits the air and burns up. Find it earlier in the same sentence.
items.explain: "They" means the bits of dust. The bits of dust hit the air, and then they burn up and make streaks of light. It is in the first paragraph.

items.prompt: Read: "She told them that they would not need a telescope, because meteors move too fast and cover too much of the sky." Who is "She"?
items.hint: Three people in this story are "she". Read the sentence before. Ask who invited the others and would tell them what to bring.
items.explain: "She" means Dr. Lee. Dr. Lee invited Priya and Maya in the sentence before, and she told them they would not need a telescope. It is in the second paragraph.

items.prompt: Read: "After about twenty minutes, Maya saw the first one, and she called out its direction." Whose direction did Maya call out?
items.hint: "Its" means something belongs to a thing. Ask what "the first one" means. They were waiting to count something.
items.explain: "Its" means the first meteor's. Maya saw the first meteor, and she called out which way the meteor went. It is at the end of the second paragraph.

items.prompt: Each sentence has "she" or "her". Put it under the person that the word means.

cards.text: Dr. Lee invited Priya and Maya to count meteors with her.
She told them that they would not need a telescope.
She called out its direction.
She kept count on a clipboard.
She could write down how many meteors they had seen.

items.hint: Find each sentence in the story. If the sentence has a name, ask whether the pronoun means that person or someone else.
items.explain: Dr. Lee invited the girls to count with her, told them they would not need a telescope and wrote down how many meteors they saw. Priya kept count on the clipboard. Maya saw the first meteor and called out its direction.

items.prompt: Read: "Then he led the group down a long tunnel into the hill." Who is "he"?
items.hint: Three people in this paragraph are "he". Read the first two sentences. Ask what job each person has.
items.explain: "He" means Mr. Varga. Mr. Varga guides the tours, and Ben and Sam joined his tour, so he led the group. It is at the end of the first paragraph.

items.prompt: Read: "They broke the rock with hammers and drills, and then they loaded it into small carts." Who are "They"?
options: the miners from about a hundred years ago
the people on the ten o'clock tour
items.hint: "They" means more than one. The tour group is also more than one. Read the sentence before to find who broke rock long ago.
items.explain: "They" means the miners from about a hundred years ago. The sentence before says the miners worked in these tunnels for ten hours a day. It is in the second paragraph.

items.prompt: Read: "Ben was surprised at how heavy it was, even when it was empty." What does "it" mean?
items.hint: "It" means one thing. Read the sentence before. Ask which thing the boys pushed and could be empty.
items.explain: "It" means the old cart. Mr. Varga let the boys push the cart, and Ben was surprised that the cart was heavy even when it was empty. It is at the end of the second paragraph.

items.prompt: Read: "He explained that the early miners worked by the light of candles, so this was what they saw whenever a candle went out." What does "this" mean?
options: the complete darkness in the tunnel
the lamp on a hard hat
items.hint: "This" points back to something the group had just seen. Read the sentence before.
items.explain: "This" means the complete darkness in the tunnel. The tunnel became completely dark, and that is what the miners saw when a candle went out. It is in the last paragraph.

items.prompt: Read: "No person drives it with a steering wheel." What does "it" mean?
items.hint: In the first sentence, "it" means Mars. Ask which thing could be driven.
items.explain: "It" means the rover. A rover is a robot that drives across Mars, and no person drives the rover with a steering wheel. It is in the first paragraph.

items.prompt: Rewrite the sentence. Choose what "They" and "them" mean.
items.frame: {0} take pictures of the ground ahead, and the rover uses {1} to choose a safe path.
items.hint: Read the sentence before. Ask which things can take pictures. Then ask what the rover could use to choose a path.
items.explain: The cameras take pictures of the ground ahead, and the rover uses the pictures to choose a safe path. The sentence before names the cameras on the mast.

items.prompt: Read: "Because of this delay, the rover must be able to make some decisions on its own." What is "this delay"?
options: the minutes a radio message takes to get to Mars
the time the rover takes to roll over rocks
the time the arm takes to drill into a rock
the years before a future mission comes
items.hint: "This" points back to something already named. Read the sentence before. Ask what takes a long time.
items.explain: "This delay" means the minutes a radio message takes to get to Mars. The sentence before says a message can take more than ten minutes. It is in the first paragraph.

items.prompt: Read the last sentence: "They are looking for clues about whether Mars once had lakes and rivers." Who are "They"?
items.hint: "They" can mean people or things. Read the sentence before. Ask who studies the pictures and could look for clues.
items.explain: "They" means the scientists on Earth. The sentence before says scientists study the pictures and test results, and they look for clues about lakes and rivers.

items.prompt: Read: "They take turns standing at the colder outer edge, so no single bird stays cold for too long." Who are "They"?
items.hint: "They" means more than one. Read the sentence before. Find the group that is standing together on the ice.
items.explain: "They" means the males in the huddle. Thousands of males crowd together, and they take turns at the cold outer edge. It is at the end of the second paragraph.

items.prompt: Read: "If she has not returned yet, its father feeds it a milky liquid that he makes in his throat." What does "it" mean?
items.hint: Read the sentence before. Ask what has just hatched and needs to eat.
items.explain: "It" means the chick. The sentence before says the chick hatches while its mother is still at sea, so the father feeds the chick. It is in the third paragraph.

items.prompt: Read: "This small meal gives the chick enough food for a few more days." What is "this small meal"?
options: the milky liquid from the father's throat
the fish and squid that the mother catches
the food from the mother's stomach
items.hint: "This" points back to something just named. Read the sentence before.
items.explain: "This small meal" means the milky liquid that the father makes in his throat. It is named in the sentence before, in the third paragraph.

items.prompt: Each sentence has "she" or "he". Put it under the parent that the word means.

cards.text: She cannot keep the egg warm for long.
He covers the egg with a warm fold of skin.
He does not eat at all for about two months.
She finds her partner by listening for his call.
She feeds the chick food from her stomach.
He finally walks to the sea to eat.

items.hint: "She" means a female and "he" means a male. Find each sentence in the article and ask which parent does it.
items.explain: The mother cannot keep the egg warm, finds her partner by his call and feeds the chick from her stomach. The father covers the egg, does not eat for about two months and finally walks to the sea to eat.

items.prompt: Read: "As this air climbs, it cools, and the water in it forms tall clouds." What does "it" mean?
options: the warm, wet air rising from the sea
items.hint: "This air" points back to the sentence before. Ask what is climbing and cooling.
items.explain: "It" means the warm, wet air rising from the sea. The sentence before says the air rises, and as it climbs, it cools. It is in the second paragraph.

items.prompt: Read: "More air rushes in across the water to take its place." Whose place is "its place"?
options: the place of the warm air that rose
the place of the ocean water
items.hint: Something moved away and left a space. Read the sentences before. Ask what was rising up from the sea.
items.explain: "Its place" means the place of the warm air that rose. The warm air rises faster and faster, so more air rushes in to fill the space it left. It is in the second paragraph.

items.prompt: Read: "This process releases heat, which makes the air rise even faster." What does "This process" mean?
options: the water in the rising air forming clouds
more air rushing in across the water
items.hint: "This" points back to the sentence just before. Find what is happening in that sentence.
items.explain: "This process" means the water in the rising air forming clouds. The sentence just before tells about it, in the second paragraph.

items.prompt: Read: "They can blow faster than 150 miles per hour in the strongest storms." What does "They" mean?
options: the light winds in the eye
items.hint: "They" can mean things. Ask what can blow. Then read the sentence before to find which ones are the fastest.
items.explain: "They" means the winds in the eyewall. The sentence before says the eyewall has the fastest winds in the whole storm. It is in the third paragraph.

items.prompt: Read: "Then he skated over to Leo and gave him some advice." Who is "he"?
items.hint: This "he" skated over to Leo, so "he" is someone else. Read the sentences before to find who had just tried the trick.
items.explain: "He" means the older skater from Gull Point. He slid off the rail, stood up and laughed, and then he skated over to give Leo advice. It is in the second paragraph.

items.prompt: The third paragraph starts: "Leo had not noticed this, and he was grateful to learn it before his turn." What does "this" mean?
options: the end of the rail was a little higher than it looked
the older skater wore a bright orange helmet
the older skater's back wheels caught the rail
the skate jam was a friendly contest
items.hint: "This" points back to an idea. Read the last sentence of the paragraph before. Ask what Leo learned before his turn.
items.explain: "This" means the fact that the end of the rail was a little higher than it looked. The older skater explains it in the last sentence of the second paragraph.

items.prompt: Rewrite the last two sentences with names. Choose who each "him" and "he" means.
items.frame: Leo did not win first place, but the judges gave {0} a prize. Afterward, {1} found the older boy and thanked {2}.
items.hint: Ask who won a prize, who said thank you, and who was being thanked. You thank someone other than yourself.
items.explain: The judges gave Leo a prize. Afterward, Leo found the older boy and thanked the skater from Gull Point. It is in the last paragraph.

items.prompt: Read: "If they waited for it, they would miss the slow train, because it left only once every two hours." This sentence uses "it" two times. What does the second "it" mean?
items.hint: The first "it" is the train they would wait for. Ask which train they would miss.
items.explain: The second "it" means the slow train. They would miss the slow train, because the slow train left only once every two hours. The first "it" means the fast train. It is in the second paragraph.

items.prompt: Read: "He asked the woman at the ticket window when it left, and she told him that it would leave in ten minutes from the stop across the street." Who is "she"?
options: the woman at the ticket window
items.hint: Two women are in this part of the story. Look earlier in the same sentence. Ask who Sam asked about the bus.
items.explain: "She" means the woman at the ticket window. Sam asked her when the bus left, and she told him. It is in the third paragraph.

items.prompt: Read: "Sam explained this to his grandma, and she smiled." What does "this" mean?
options: the plan to take the bus that leaves in ten minutes
the news that the fast train was forty minutes late
the fact that the slow train left once every two hours
the route he traced on the map at home
items.hint: "This" points back to an idea. Read the two sentences before. Ask what Sam had just found out.
items.explain: "This" means the plan to take the bus that leaves in ten minutes. Sam found the bus on the map and asked when it left, and then he explained the plan to his grandma. It is in the third paragraph.

items.prompt: Each sentence has "it". Put it under the thing that "it" means.

cards.text: Sam unfolded his map again and studied it carefully.
If they waited for it, they would miss the slow train.
He noticed that it stopped right outside Valley Junction station.
He asked the woman at the ticket window when it left.
The bus was slower than the trains, but it had large windows.

items.hint: Find each sentence in the story. Ask which thing could be studied, which thing they were waiting for, and which thing stops at Valley Junction.
items.explain: Sam studied the map. They would wait for the fast train. The bus stopped outside Valley Junction station, left from the stop across the street and had large windows.

items.prompt: Read: "When the yeast eats the flour, it gives off a gas, and the gas makes bubbles in the dough." What does "it" mean?
items.hint: Ask what is eating and then giving off gas. Find it earlier in the same sentence.
items.explain: "It" means the yeast. The yeast eats the flour, and then the yeast gives off a gas. It is in the first paragraph.

items.prompt: The third paragraph starts: "Sam called his grandma to ask about this." What does "this" mean?
options: why the starter smelled a little sour
how to feed the starter every morning
when the school fair would start
items.hint: "This" points back to a question. Read the last sentence of the paragraph before.
items.explain: "This" means why the starter smelled a little sour. Ben wondered about it at the end of the second paragraph, and Sam called his grandma to ask.

items.prompt: Rewrite the sentence with names. Choose who "she", "her" and "he" mean.
items.frame: In March, {0} gave Sam a small jar of {1} starter so that {2} could bake bread for the school fair.
items.hint: Read the first sentence of the story. Find whose bakery has the starter. Then ask who got the jar.
items.explain: In March, Grandma Rose gave Sam a small jar of Grandma Rose's starter so that Sam could bake bread for the school fair. The first sentence says the starter is at her bakery.

items.prompt: Read: "Ben's mom asked them for the recipe, and Sam promised to bring her a jar of starter too." Who is "her"?
items.hint: Two women are in this story. Look earlier in the same sentence. Ask who wanted the recipe.
items.explain: "Her" means Ben's mom. She asked for the recipe, so Sam promised to bring her a jar of starter. It is the last sentence.

items.prompt: Read: "Many of them hurried to the rail, and Maya, who was traveling to the island with her sketchbook, found a spot near the front." Who are "them"?
items.hint: "Them" means more than one. Read the sentence before. Ask who heard the captain on the speaker.
items.explain: "Them" means the passengers. The captain told the passengers about the whales, and many of them hurried to the rail. It is in the second paragraph.

items.prompt: Read: "During that time, it learns the long routes that humpback whales travel between their feeding and breeding waters." What does "it" mean?
items.hint: Read the sentence before. Ask who stays with its mother for about a year and has things to learn.
items.explain: "It" means the humpback calf. The sentence before says the calf stays beside its mother for about a year, and during that time it learns the routes. It is in the third paragraph.

items.prompt: Read: "She added the puffs of mist, the waves and the green hills of the island in the background." Who is "She"?
items.hint: Two people in this story are "she". Read the sentence before. Ask who was drawing.
items.explain: "She" means Maya. Maya drew the whales in the sentence before, and then she added the mist, the waves and the hills. It is in the third paragraph.

items.prompt: Read the last sentence: "It is still there today." What does "It" mean?
items.hint: Read the sentence before. Ask what was put in a place. "There" is that place.
items.explain: "It" means Maya's drawing. Captain Lane pinned the drawing beside the ticket window, and the drawing is still there today.

items.prompt: Read: "Its thin wheels had sunk deep into the sand, and they spun without moving it forward." What does "they" mean?
items.hint: Ask what can spin. Then look earlier in the same sentence.
items.explain: "They" means the rover's thin wheels. The wheels sank into the sand, and they spun without moving the rover. It is at the end of the first paragraph.

items.prompt: Read: "Priya liked this idea, but she pointed out that they had no wide wheels in the club's parts box." What does "this idea" mean?
options: using wide wheels so the rover would not sink
cutting rings from a plastic bottle
driving the rover faster across the sand
asking Ms. Ortiz for new wheels
items.hint: "This" points back to an idea that was already named. Read the two sentences before.
items.explain: "This idea" means using wide wheels so the rover would not sink. Maya described the truck with wide tires, and the next sentence explains why wide tires work. The bottle rings come later, in the third paragraph.

items.prompt: Read: "Priya fixed them in place with tape, and then she set the rover at the edge of the sand again." What does "them" mean?
options: the parts in the club's box
items.hint: "Them" means more than one thing. Read the sentence before. Ask what Maya had just made that needed to stay in place.
items.explain: "Them" means the four plastic rings. Maya slid a ring over each wheel, and Priya taped the rings in place. It is in the third paragraph.

items.prompt: Each sentence has "she" or "her". Put it under the person that the word means.

cards.text: She remembered a photo of a desert truck with very wide tires.
She pointed out that they had no wide wheels in the parts box.
She cut four rings from an old plastic bottle.
She set the rover at the edge of the sand again.
Priya said that the bottle rings were her partner's idea.
She wrote their solution on the board.

items.hint: Find each sentence in the story. If the sentence has a name, ask whether the pronoun means that person or someone else.
items.explain: Maya remembered the truck photo and cut the bottle rings. Priya pointed out there were no wide wheels, set the rover down again and said the rings were her partner's idea. Ms. Ortiz wrote the solution on the board.

items.prompt: Read: "This made the creek muddy, and the fish that live there need clear water." What does "This" mean?
options: the soil on the bank washing into the water
the roots holding the soil in place
the fish swimming in the creek
items.hint: "This" points back to the sentence just before. Ask what could make water muddy.
items.explain: "This" means the soil on the bank washing into the water. Soil in the water makes the creek muddy. It is in the first paragraph.

items.prompt: Read: "Thirty of them came on a Saturday morning, along with Ms. Ortiz and Mr. Okafor, who brought a box of work gloves." Who are "them"?
options: the students at Harbor Middle School
items.hint: "Them" means more than one. Read the sentence before. Ask who was invited to come and help.
items.explain: "Them" means the students at Harbor Middle School. The ranger invited the students to help, and thirty of them came. It is in the second paragraph.

items.prompt: Rewrite the last sentence with names. Choose who "he" and "him" mean.
items.frame: The ranger laughed and said that {0} would be glad to show {1} around.
items.hint: Read the sentence before. Ask who wants to come back in ten years, and who works in the woods.
items.explain: The ranger laughed and said that the ranger would be glad to show Mr. Okafor around. Mr. Okafor said he would come back in the sentence before, and the ranger works in the woods.

items.prompt: Read: "Their roots, however, would begin to hold the bank together much sooner, probably in only a year or two." What does "Their" mean?
items.hint: In the first paragraph, "their roots" meant other trees. Read the sentence just before this one.
items.explain: "Their" means the new trees'. The sentence before is about the new trees, and their roots will soon hold the bank together. It is in the last paragraph.

items.prompt: Read: "The boy from Gull Point shook his hand and said that it was the hardest game he had played all year." Whose hand did he shake?
options: a player at the next table's
items.hint: You shake someone else's hand. Ask who the boy from Gull Point had just played.
items.explain: He shook Ben's hand. The boy from Gull Point had just played Ben, so "his hand" means Ben's hand. It is in the last paragraph.

items.prompt: Rewrite the sentence. Choose who or what "His", "it" and "he" mean.
items.frame: {0} opponent had not noticed {1}, because {2} was busy attacking Ben's king.

slots.label: it
options: Ben's pawn near the far side

slots.label: he
options: a player at the next table

items.hint: Find what Ben noticed, two sentences before. Then ask who Ben was playing against.
items.explain: Ben's opponent had not noticed Ben's pawn near the far side, because the boy from Gull Point was busy attacking Ben's king. It is in the third paragraph.

items.prompt: Read: "On the bus home, Ben told Ana that her advice had saved the game." What was her advice?
options: to stop looking at what he had lost and look for what he could still do
to push the pawn forward twice
to watch the chess clock closely
items.hint: Find who "her" means. Then look back in the second paragraph for what that person told Ben at breakfast.
items.explain: Ana's advice was to stop looking at what he had lost and look for what he could still do. Ana told Ben this at breakfast, at the end of the second paragraph.

items.prompt: Read: "This change takes millions of years, and it happens only when conditions are just right." What is "This change"?
options: an animal dying near a river
wind and rain wearing away rock
items.hint: "This" points back to the sentence before. Find something that changes from one thing into another.
items.explain: "This change" means bones slowly turning into stone. The first sentence tells about it, in the first paragraph.

items.prompt: Read: "When it seeps into a buried bone, the minerals fill the tiny holes and spaces inside it." This sentence uses "it" two times. What does the first "it" mean?
options: the water moving through the rock
items.hint: The second "it" is the thing with holes inside. Read the sentence before. Ask what can move and seep into a bone.
items.explain: The first "it" means the water moving through the rock. The water seeps into the bone, and the minerals fill the holes inside the bone. It is in the third paragraph.

items.prompt: Read: "Little by little, they harden, and the bone becomes a copy made of stone." What does "they" mean?
options: the soft parts of the body
items.hint: "They" means more than one thing. Read the sentence before. Ask what filled the holes in the bone.
items.explain: "They" means the minerals. The minerals fill the holes in the bone, and then they harden into stone. It is at the end of the third paragraph.

items.prompt: Read: "Over time, more layers of mud pile up on top of them, and their weight slowly presses the lower layers into rock." Whose weight presses the lower layers into rock?
options: the soft parts of the body
items.hint: This sentence has "them" and "their", and they mean different things. "Them" is what is buried. Ask what is piling up on top.
items.explain: "Their weight" means the weight of the new layers of mud. The layers pile up on top of the bones, and their weight presses the lower layers into rock. "Them" means the bones and teeth.

steps.say: I see the word 'She'. 'She' means a girl or a woman.
I look back for a name that comes before it.
The first sentence names Priya. Priya is the only person in this story.
